  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Learning properties of neural networks has recently attracted growing interest, with existing approaches operating either directly on network parameters or through probe-based representations of network behavior. While probing methods have shown strong empirical performance, their theoretical foundations remain limited.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">In this work, we study when finite probe-based representations are sufficient for learning neural functionals. We establish general identification and universality results for probing, and show that using intermediate hidden representations can provide significantly more informative representations than relying only on final outputs. Motivated by these results, we introduce <span id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span>, a simple architecture for learning from hidden probe responses. Across a range of neural functional benchmarks, including both MLPs and Transformers, <span id="abstract1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> consistently improves over existing probing methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance. Our code is publicly available on <a href="https://github.com/yonatansverdlov/HiddenProbe" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">GitHub</a>.</p>
  
</div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the topic of learning neural functionals (also known as weight space learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al. (2026)</a></cite>). A neural functional is a mapping <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> taking a neural network <math id="S1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to a vector <math id="S1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi(\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi(\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, one could consider a neural functional predicting the test accuracy of a given neural network. Another example is where <math id="S1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is an INR representing an image, and then standard image tasks like image classification become neural functionals.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A popular approach to learning neural functionals <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi(f_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi(f_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> is via <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">weight space methods</em>, which think of the functionals as a function of the parameters <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\psi}(\theta)=\psi(f_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>ψ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\psi}(\theta)=\psi(f_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>, and then apply neural architectures directly to the parameter weights to learn <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ψ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math>. Several recent works have adopted this approach with some success <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Navon et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2023b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2023a)</a></cite>.
However, weight-space learning must contend with the fact that many distinct parameter vectors can represent the same function. Accounting for these parameter symmetries is often important for performance, but typically requires symmetry-aware architectures that are more complex to design and implement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Probing provides an alternative way to process neural models that avoids the parameterization ambiguities of weight-space methods. Rather than representing <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> through its parameters <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, probing represents it through its evaluations on a set of inputs, called probes, <math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}</annotation></semantics></math>. The learning problem is then to find a function <math id="S1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\psi}\bigl(f_{\theta}(p_{1}),\ldots,f_{\theta}(p_{N})\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>ψ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\psi}\bigl(f_{\theta}(p_{1}),\ldots,f_{\theta}(p_{N})\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math>
that approximates the desired neural functional <math id="S1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi(f_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi(f_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Probe-based methods, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al. (2025)</a></cite>, have achieved strong empirical performance on several benchmarks, but currently lack a theoretical justification. In particular, while weight space methods like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Navon et al. (2023)</a></cite> can provably approximate all neural functionals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dayan et al. (2026)</a></cite>, analogous universality guarantees are not known for probe-based methods. Moreover, whereas the parameters <math id="S1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> fully specify <math id="S1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, a finite probe set reveals only the values of <math id="S1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> at finitely many inputs and therefore appears, a priori, to provide only partial information about the realized function. This raises two closely related questions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Main Questions:</span></p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Can a function <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> be uniquely reconstructed from a finite number of probes? If so, how many probes are needed?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Can any neural functional <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda(f_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda(f_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> be approximated by a probe-based model?</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Main Results:</span>
As we shall see, our answer to both questions will be positive. Under the assumption that <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is analytic, we show that the function <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> can be uniquely recovered from <math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2q+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2q+1</annotation></semantics></math> probes, where <math id="S1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the dimension of the parameter space. As a result, we will show that any neural functions <math id="S1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda(f_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda(f_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> can be approximated by a probe-based model with <math id="S1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2q+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2q+1</annotation></semantics></math> probes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, we will discuss probe based methods which represent <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> not only through the final probe value <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}(p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}(p)</annotation></semantics></math>, but also through the value of all intermediate layers on the probes. For both MLP and self-attention, we will show that this representation requires fewer probes to obtain the same guarantees. For fully connected neural networks, this brings down the sufficient probe count from <math id="S1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(q)</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(d_{\max})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(d_{\max})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> is the maximal width, and for self-attention blocks this brings down the count to <math id="S1.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(d_{in}h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(d_{in}h)</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S1.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{in}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{in}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> being the input dimension and number of heads, respectively.
Motivated by this we suggest a specialized model to learn properties of neural networks with such probes, which we name <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Empirically, we will show that <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> attains state of the art results on several standard neural functional datasets.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.33901v2/paper_plots/hiddenprobe_overview.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:439/201;" width="439" height="201" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overview of HiddenProbe.</span>
A set of learnable probes <math id="S1.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}</annotation></semantics></math> is evaluated on a target neural network <math id="S1.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, producing intermediate activations <math id="S1.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}(p_{j},\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}(p_{j},\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> and final outputs <math id="S1.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{L}(p_{j},\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{L}(p_{j},\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>, which are processed by an invariant model and an MLP to predict a property of the target network.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>Previous Work</h3>

<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Weight-space learning.</h5>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Weight-space learning studies models that process the parameters of other neural networks directly; we refer to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al. (2026)</a></cite> for a recent survey. A central challenge in this setting is that different parameterizations can represent the same function, motivating architectures that explicitly respect weight-space symmetries. DWSNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Navon et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and Neural Functional Networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023a</a>)</cite> construct linear layers equivariant to hidden-neuron permutations, while Neural Functional Transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023b</a>)</cite> incorporate the same symmetry into attention-based architectures. More recent graph-based approaches, including Graph Metanetworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lim et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Neural Graphs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, represent networks as computational graphs, enabling weight-space processing across a broader range of architectures.
Beyond permutations, subsequent methods incorporate additional symmetries, such as ScaleGMN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalogeropoulos et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Monomial-NFN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which account for scaling and sign symmetries induced by particular activation functions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Identification and learning from probes</h5>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work in weight-space learning has explored combining network weights with responses to input probes to predict network properties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Herrmann et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Complementary approaches rely solely on final outputs evaluated at learned probes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Beyond weight-space learning, interpolation and identification of neural-network from input–output observations has also been studied in learning theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vardi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. More recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhattamishra et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim and Kim (2026)</a></cite> have investigated recovering the weights of frozen transformers from query outputs. Beyond final outputs, hidden activations provide additional information about a network’s internal representations. Prior work has used these activations to study representation properties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alain and Bengio, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cotler et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and, more recently, to investigate model behavior through mechanistic interpretability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gurnee et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
In natural language processing, probing classifiers similarly predict
linguistic properties from a model’s hidden representations to study
the information they encode <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belinkov, 2022</a>)</cite>.
Within weight-space learning, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heo et al. (2026)</a></cite> similarly probe selected hidden layers to predict network properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To the best of our knowledge, prior work has not systematically studied property prediction from complete activation traces across all hidden layers, collected by evaluating a network on input probes. We address this gap by studying when neural functions can be identified from the activations induced by input queries, and how universal approximators can be designed to predict network properties from final outputs and hidden activation traces.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.2 </span>Preliminaries</h3>

<div id="S1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consider a parametric family
<math id="S1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathcal{X}\times\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathcal{X}\times\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> is the input domain and
<math id="S1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{q}</annotation></semantics></math> is the parameter domain.
Every fixed parameter <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\in\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\in\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> defines a function
<math id="S1.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}(x)=f(x;\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}(x)=f(x;\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>.
We use <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\cdot;\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\cdot;\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> interchangeably.
We denote the collection of all such functions by
<math id="S1.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our motivating application is the problem of learning neural functionals<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            Our focus is on neural functionals which depend only on the function <math id="footnotex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> and not on the specific parameterization <math id="footnotex2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. In the terminology of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dayan et al. (2026)</a></cite> these are called function-space functionals</span></span></span><math id="S1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi:\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi:\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, and our focus is on analyzing methods which rely on probing. We will now define these methods, and focus on two variants: final-layer probing and hidden-layer probing.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Final-layer probing</h5>

<div id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Final-layer probing represents a function <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> by considering its output on a number of input points, called probes. Formally, given an <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> tuple of points <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}\coloneqq(p_{1},\cdots,p_{N})\in\mathcal{X}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}\coloneqq(p_{1},\cdots,p_{N})\in\mathcal{X}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, the model <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is mapped to an <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\times N</annotation></semantics></math> dimensional matrix</p>
<table id="S1.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi_{\text{final}}(\mathcal{P};\theta)\coloneqq(f_{\theta}(p_{1}),\cdots,f_{\theta}(p_{N}))\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mtext>final</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi_{\text{final}}(\mathcal{P};\theta)\coloneqq(f_{\theta}(p_{1}),\cdots,f_{\theta}(p_{N}))\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This matrix is processed to learn properties of the neural network, e.g., by applying an MLP <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{\text{MLP}}\circ\Psi_{\text{final}}(\mathcal{P};\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mtext>MLP</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mtext>final</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{\text{MLP}}\circ\Psi_{\text{final}}(\mathcal{P};\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> to the output, to obtain a neural model for learning the functional <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda(f_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda(f_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>. A representative example of this approach is the ProbeGen method of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al. (2025)</a></cite>, which uses this approach precisely with a carefully designed method for learning the probes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hidden-Layer Probing</h5>

<div id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heo et al. (2026)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horwitz et al. (2025)</a></cite>,
In applications, the parametric functions <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> are typically constructed by a composition of simpler functions (e.g. layers), that is
<math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}=f_{L,\theta}\circ\ldots\circ f_{2,\theta}\circ f_{1,\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}=f_{L,\theta}\circ\ldots\circ f_{2,\theta}\circ f_{1,\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>. When this compositional structure is present, hidden layer probing relates to the practice of retaining the output of all intermediate computations on the probes, and not only the final output. Formally, for every input <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> and parameter <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\in\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\in\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> we define</p>

<section id="S1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.3 </span>Overview</h3>

<div id="S1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the remainder of the paper, we will prove that analytic neural networks of any kind can be identified by a number of final-layer probes proportional to the network’s parameters (Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Identifying Analytic Neural Networks from Probe evaluations ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), and will show, for both MLPs and transformers, that the required number of probes can be greatly reduced when allowing Hidden-Layer probing (Sections <a href="#S3" title="3 Probing MLPs ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>-<a href="#S4" title="4 Identifying Multi-Head Attention from Probes ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). We then describe <span id="S1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span>, a method for learning using hidden probes (Section <a href="#S5" title="5 HiddenProbe: Learning using Hidden Neural Activations ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), prove the universality of probe-based methods (Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Universality of probe-based learning ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), and finally demonstrate the effectiveness of <span id="S1.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> on neural functional learning (Section <a href="#S7" title="7 Experiments ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Identifying Analytic Neural Networks from Probe evaluations</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our first result is that final-layer probe evaluations are enough to identify <em id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">analytic</em> parametric functions, and the number of probes is proportional to the dimension of the parameter space. This theorem applies to all analytic parametric families including MLPs and Transformers, provided that the activations used in these models are analytic. Examples of such activations are tanh, sigmoid, SiLU and sine activations.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Unique reconstruction from finite samples)<span id="Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> be an analytic function. Then, for almost any choice of probes <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1},\ldots,p_{2q+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1},\ldots,p_{2q+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, we have that for all
<math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\in\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\in\Theta</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S2.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="f(p_{j},\theta_{1})=f(p_{j},\theta_{2}),\forall j=1,\ldots,2q+1\Longleftrightarrow\ f(\cdot,\theta_{1})\equiv f(\cdot,\theta_{2})\ \text{on }\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.778em" stretchy="false">⟺</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.500em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">on </mtext><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(p_{j},\theta_{1})=f(p_{j},\theta_{2}),\forall j=1,\ldots,2q+1\Longleftrightarrow\ f(\cdot,\theta_{1})\equiv f(\cdot,\theta_{2})\ \text{on }\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof Idea.</h6>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">Intuitively we can interpret this result as follows: although the family of functions <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{f_{\theta}|\quad\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{q}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>q</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{f_{\theta}|\quad\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{q}\}</annotation></semantics></math> contains infinitely many functions, it has a finite dimensional parameterization in <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>q</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{q}</annotation></semantics></math>, and so it is reasonable that a finite number of <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim q</annotation></semantics></math> evaluations can separate the realized functions. This is similar to the well-known result that a degree <math id="S2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> polynomial can be identified by <math id="S2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n+1</annotation></semantics></math> samples. However, this rule of thumb is not always true. For example, for ReLU networks, no finite number of probes suffices to uniquely identify the function (see Subsection <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Identifying ReLU Networks from Probe evaluations ‣ 3 Probing MLPs ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>). The proof that such a result does hold for analytic functions is based on the Finite Witness Theorem by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amir et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Universality of probe-based learning ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> we will show that this result implies universal approximation: probe based methods with <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2q+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2q+1</annotation></semantics></math> probes can approximate all neural functionals. This result is substantial, since probe based methods typically use a small number of probes, while apriori it would seem that universal approximation would require an exhaustive sampling of the input domain. At the same time, the number of probes suggested by the theorem is still much larger than what is used in practice. To alleviate this disadvantage, we will next focus on hidden probes, where function identification is possible with a much lower probe cardinality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Probing MLPs</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section we specialize to the case where <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(x;\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x;\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> is an MLP. The main message of this section is that hidden probes substantially reduce the number of probes necessary to identify an MLP.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We begin our discussion by setting our notation for the MLP model class. An MLP <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(p;\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(p;\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> is determined by a choice of activation <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and a width vector
<math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}\coloneqq(d_{0},d_{1},\cdots,d_{L-1},d_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}\coloneqq(d_{0},d_{1},\cdots,d_{L-1},d_{L})</annotation></semantics></math>. An MLP <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(p;\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(p;\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> is then defined via</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{0}\coloneqq p,\,x_{i}\coloneqq\sigma\left(W_{i}x_{i-1}+b_{i}\right),\,\forall i\in[L],\," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>≔</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0}\coloneqq p,\,x_{i}\coloneqq\sigma\left(W_{i}x_{i-1}+b_{i}\right),\,\forall i\in[L],\,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}\times d_{i-1}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}\times d_{i-1}}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math>, for <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in[L]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in[L]</annotation></semantics></math>, are the weights and biases, which together
define the parameters
<math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\coloneqq[W_{i},b_{i}]_{i\in[L]}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>≔</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\coloneqq[W_{i},b_{i}]_{i\in[L]}</annotation></semantics></math>. The intermediate features <math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> depend on <math id="S3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p,\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p,\theta</annotation></semantics></math> and so we denote them by <math id="S3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}(p,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}(p,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. The final function is defined by the last feature <math id="S3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(p,\theta)=x_{L}(p,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(p,\theta)=x_{L}(p,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. We denote the total dimension of the parameter space by <math id="S3.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathbf{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>𝐃</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathbf{D}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Hidden probes provide useful information:</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For MLPs with analytic activations, Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Unique reconstruction from finite samples). ‣ 2 Identifying Analytic Neural Networks from Probe evaluations ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> implies that a finite number of probes, proportional to <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathbf{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>𝐃</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathbf{D}}</annotation></semantics></math>, is sufficient. For hidden probes, the number of necessary probes depends only on the maximal width:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Reconstruction from hidden layer activations)<span id="Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> be an analytic, injective, non-polynomial activation. Let <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(p,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(p,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> denote an MLP with activation <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and widths <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}\coloneqq(d_{0},d_{1},\cdots,d_{L-1},d_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}\coloneqq(d_{0},d_{1},\cdots,d_{L-1},d_{L})</annotation></semantics></math>. Assume that <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N&gt;\max_{i}d_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N&gt;\max_{i}d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then for almost every <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{X}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{X}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, we have that for almost every <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{1},\theta_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{1},\theta_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi_{\text{all}}(\theta_{1},\mathcal{P})=\Psi_{\text{all}}(\theta_{2},\mathcal{P})\implies\,\theta_{1}=\theta_{2},\,\implies f(\cdot,\theta_{1})=f(\cdot,\theta_{2})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">all</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">all</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.448em" stretchy="false">⟹</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo stretchy="false">⟹</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi_{\text{all}}(\theta_{1},\mathcal{P})=\Psi_{\text{all}}(\theta_{2},\mathcal{P})\implies\,\theta_{1}=\theta_{2},\,\implies f(\cdot,\theta_{1})=f(\cdot,\theta_{2}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this result we add the assumption that the activation is non-polynomial and injective (this is the case for e.g., tanh and sigmoid, but not for sine activation). Moreover, identifiability is not on the whole domain, but rather it holds for parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{1},\theta_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{1},\theta_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> outside an exceptional Lebesgue-null set <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math>. The proof in fact shows a stronger statement: the set <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> is a zero set of an analytic function, and hence is of strictly lower dimension than the parameter space, and has empty interior. In general, whenever we talk about ”almost everywhere” in this paper, this stronger notion applies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof Idea.</h6>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">The idea of the proof is based on a straightforward algorithm described in detail in in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title='Algorithm 1 ‣ Algorithm to recover weights from Ψ_"all" for generic targets ‣ B.1 Identification of Analytic MLPs from Hidden Probes ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> of Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Identification of Analytic MLPs from Hidden Probes ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>. Intuitively, the parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i},b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i},b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> of the <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th layer satisfy the linear equations</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\sigma^{-1}\left(x_{i}(p_{j},\theta)\right)=W_{i}x_{i-1}(p_{j},\theta)+b_{i},\quad j=1,\ldots,N" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{-1}\left(x_{i}(p_{j},\theta)\right)=W_{i}x_{i-1}(p_{j},\theta)+b_{i},\quad j=1,\ldots,N</annotation></semantics></math></td>
