</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text">The proof shows that for generic probes and parameters, these linear equations have a unique solution.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tightness of results</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Lower bounds on probe counts ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a> we give examples of analytic MLPs that cannot be identified with <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> hidden probes (exactly matching the bound of Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2 (Reconstruction from hidden layer activations). ‣ 3.1 Hidden probes provide useful information: ‣ 3 Probing MLPs ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) For final-layer probes, we construct, for every
<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\leq 2q_{D}-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\leq 2q_{D}-2</annotation></semantics></math>, a nonempty open set of probe tuples that
fail to separate all realized functions. (Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Unique reconstruction from finite samples). ‣ 2 Identifying Analytic Neural Networks from Probe evaluations ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> gives a sufficient bound of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2q_{\mathbf{D}}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>𝐃</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2q_{\mathbf{D}}+1</annotation></semantics></math> generic probes).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Identifying ReLU Networks from Probe evaluations</h3>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:35%;"><img src="2609.33901v2/paper_plots/hat.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:192/159;" width="192" height="159" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>For any finite set of probes, a nonzero ReLU ‘hat’ function can be constructed whose support avoids all probes.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our results on identifiability of an MLP from a finite number of probes require analytic activations, and thus do not apply to the common ReLU activation. In fact, such a result is not possible for ReLU activations:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 3</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Finite probes do not identify ReLU networks)<span id="Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For any finite set of probes <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, there exist two distinct ReLU networks, each with three hidden neurons, that agree on all the probes. Consequently, no finite set of probes can uniquely identify all ReLU networks.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof Idea.</h6>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">For given probes <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, it is possible to construct two different hat functions which are zero on the probes: for example, the functions plotted in blue and orange in <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Identifying ReLU Networks from Probe evaluations ‣ 3 Probing MLPs ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a>. Full proof is in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 ReLU Network Identification from probes ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Since exact identification of ReLU networks from finitely many probes is impossible, we instead study approximate identification in <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}(\mu)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}(\mu)</annotation></semantics></math>. We show that, with probability at least <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\delta</annotation></semantics></math> over the sampled probes, any network that agrees with the target network on those probes is within <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> of the target in <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}(\mu)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}(\mu)</annotation></semantics></math>. This is similar in spirit to results from PAC learning. The following theorem gives a semi-formal description of these results, which are described and proved in more detail in Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem11" title="Theorem 11 (PAC identification of ReLU networks). ‣ Proof of the formal version of Theorem : ‣ B.3 ReLU Network Identification from probes ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> of Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 ReLU Network Identification from probes ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 4</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(semi-formal-PAC identification of <math id="Thmtheorem4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{ReLU}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ReLU</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{ReLU}</annotation></semantics></math> networks)<span id="Thmtheorem4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmtheorem4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Consider the family of <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{ReLU}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ReLU</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{ReLU}</annotation></semantics></math> MLPs with widths <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}\coloneqq(d_{0},d_{1},\cdots,d_{L-1},d_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}\coloneqq(d_{0},d_{1},\cdots,d_{L-1},d_{L})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> parameters. Let <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> be a compactly supported probability distribution on <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and assume that the parameter set is compact. Fix <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> and a parameter vector <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then there exist constants <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{1}(\epsilon,\delta),\,C_{2}(\epsilon,\delta)&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{1}(\epsilon,\delta),\,C_{2}(\epsilon,\delta)&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For </span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{1}=C_{1}\cdot Lq\ln(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{1}=C_{1}\cdot Lq\ln(q)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> final layer samples, with probability of at least </span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\delta</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text alttext="\theta_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{0}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> on the samples will satisfy </span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|f(\cdot;\theta)-f(\cdot;\theta_{0})\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}\leq\epsilon." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|f(\cdot;\theta)-f(\cdot;\theta_{0})\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}\leq\epsilon.</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">When hidden layer samples are used, only </span><math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{2}=C_{2}\cdot q\ln(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{2}=C_{2}\cdot q\ln(q)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> samples are sufficient.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As in the analytic activation case, this result suggests that hidden activations can reduce the number of probes necessary to (almost) identify a ReLU network, especially for deeper ReLU nets. An experimental verification of this is given in the Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Function-level reconstruction on synthetic neural networks ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Identifying Multi-Head Attention from Probes</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-head attention (MHA) forms the backbone of modern transformer architectures. In this section we discuss the identification of multiple-layer multihead attention (MHA) blocks from probes. Additional components typically used in transformers, like FFNs and LayerNorm, are omitted for mathematical tractability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">We begin with some basic definitions (details in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Function-level identification of multi-head attention ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>). We consider <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> dimensional inputs and <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> attention heads. An MHA layer
has parameters <math id="S4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\coloneqq\{(\mathbf{Q}_{a},\mathbf{K}_{a},\mathbf{V}_{a},\mathbf{O}_{a})\}_{a=1}^{h}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>≔</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐊</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐕</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐎</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>h</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\coloneqq\{(\mathbf{Q}_{a},\mathbf{K}_{a},\mathbf{V}_{a},\mathbf{O}_{a})\}_{a=1}^{h},</annotation></semantics></math>
For an input probe <math id="S4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> whose rows are the
token vectors <math id="S4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}^{\top},\ldots,p_{n}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}^{\top},\ldots,p_{n}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>, the layer computes</p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>

<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">The softmax acts rowwise:<math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left[\operatorname{softmax}(P\mathbf{M}_{a}P^{\top})\right]_{ij}=\frac{\exp(p_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{a}p_{j})}{\sum_{s=1}^{n}\exp(p_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{a}p_{s})}." display="inline" A probe specifies <math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> and returns the complete matrix
<math id="S4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{n}(P;\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{n}(P;\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>. We denote by <math id="S4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo <p id="S4.p3.3" class="ltx_p">Thus <math id="S4.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{L,n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{L,n}</annotation></semantics></math> is the stack’s final output. For a collection of probes
<math id="S4.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\mathcal{P}}=(P^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\mathcal{P}}=(P^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, where
<math id="S4.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>. As usual, we define the output-only and
hidden-access probe maps for transformers by <math id="S4.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi_{\text{final}}(\bm{\theta},\mathcal{P})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mtext>final</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi_{\text{final}}(\bm{\theta},\mathcal{P})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi_{\text{all}}(\bm{\theta},\mathcal{P})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mtext>all</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi_{\text{all}}(\bm{\theta},\mathcal{P})</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Since the softmax attention is analytic, we can apply a variant of Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Unique reconstruction from finite samples). ‣ 2 Identifying Analytic Neural Networks from Probe evaluations ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, by using the Finite Witness Theorem for the effective manifold dimension of <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> to give function-level identification from probes:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmcorollary1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmcorollary1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 1</span></span><span id="Thmcorollary1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Generic probes)<span id="Thmcorollary1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmcorollary1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fix a token length <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math>. For almost every tuple of
<math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1+2q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1+2q</annotation></semantics></math> probes in <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> and all
<math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi_{\text{final}}(\theta)=\Psi_{\text{final}}(\theta^{\prime}),\,\iff\,x_{L,n}(\cdot;\theta)\equiv x_{L,n}(\cdot;\theta^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">final</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">final</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo rspace="0.448em" stretchy="false">⇔</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi_{\text{final}}(\theta)=\Psi_{\text{final}}(\theta^{\prime}),\,\iff\,x_{L,n}(\cdot;\theta)\equiv x_{L,n}(\cdot;\theta^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Note that all of these parameter counts are <math id="S4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(d^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(d^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> per layer for the standard multi-head attention blocks. But softmax attention has more structure than analyticity, and we can query probes of varying token lengths to an MHA block, which lets us identify the function using only <math id="S4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(dh)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(dh)</annotation></semantics></math> probes:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem5" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 5</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Structured probing for softmax attention)<span id="Thmtheorem5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmtheorem5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\max}\coloneqq\max_{\ell}h_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>≔</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\max}\coloneqq\max_{\ell}h_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\coloneqq d(2h_{\max}+1)+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\coloneqq d(2h_{\max}+1)+1</annotation></semantics></math>. There exists an open set of probe tuples <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{X}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{X}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> of token length at most <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max\{3,1+d/h_{\max}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max\{3,1+d/h_{\max}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that for almost every target <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{0}\in\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{0}\in\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> we have:</span></p>

<div id="S4.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof Idea.</h6>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text">Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 5 (Structured probing for softmax attention). ‣ 4 Identifying Multi-Head Attention from Probes ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> gives a specific way of choosing the probes for identifying Multilayer MHA blocks with hidden access, which we call <span id="S4.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RecoverMHA</span>. We elaborate on the single layer single head case of <span id="S4.p6.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RecoverMHA</span> (see also Algorithm <a href="#alg2" title="Algorithm 2 ‣ B.4 Function-level identification of multi-head attention ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> in the appendix). In this case, the goal is to reconstruct two matrices: the matrices <math id="S4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐌</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> from (<a href="#S4.E2" title="In 4 Identifying Multi-Head Attention from Probes ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). The key trick is to do this in first stages: we first use single-token input: For such input the output of the softmax is always the scalar <math id="S4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 1}</annotation></semantics></math>, and so <math id="S4.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐌</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is eliminated, and one-token probes provide linear equations that can be used to determine <math id="S4.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>. Once <math id="S4.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> is known, we query a single probe consisting of affinely independent tokens, which uniquely recovers the attention weights for a full rank target value matrix. We then recover <math id="S4.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐌</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> from log-ratios by utilizing the softmax structure. Algorithm <a href="#alg2" title="Algorithm 2 ‣ B.4 Function-level identification of multi-head attention ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> implements these steps using
<math id="S4.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d+1</annotation></semantics></math> probes. The extension of these results to multiple heads and layers is discussed in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Function-level identification of multi-head attention ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span>: Learning using Hidden Neural Activations</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis shows that using hidden probes can greatly enhance the identifiability of neural networks from probes. Accordingly, we design a method for learning from hidden probes which we name <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span>. We have two different instantiations of this model, one for MLPs and one for transformers. The exact details are discussed in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A HiddenProbe: Probe Based learning using Hidden Neural Activations ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. However, the basic idea is simple and identical. We use learned probes, and utilize all hidden layers. The probes of each hidden layer are processed a permutation-invariant aggregator, and then the results are aggregated using a global MLP to predict the target property.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We design <span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> for MLPs so that it respects the permutation invariance of the MLP weight space. Namely, one can apply an independent permutation to the neurons of each hidden layer, and obtain a functionally equivalent MLP with permuted weight matrices. We attain permutation invariance by using permutation invariant Set Transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al. (2019)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In general, an interesting advantage of (hidden) probe methods over weight space methods is that weight space symmetries become much simpler. Indeed, while in the hidden layer representation the permutations to each hidden layer are independent, in the weight space representation these symmetries are entangled, and designing permutation invariant models for this representation can be cumbersome <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Navon et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sverdlov et al. (2025)</a></cite>. For transformers, the weight space approach needs to deal with <math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="GL(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">GL(n)</annotation></semantics></math> symmetries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al. (2025)</a></cite> which probe based methods avoid since they depend on the functional behavior of MHA and not on the exact parameterization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Universality of probe-based learning</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we use our identification results from previous sections to prove universality of probe based models with a fixed number of probes. These results are based on the standard observation that separation implies universality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dym and Gortler (2025)</a></cite>. For our theorem, we will consider analytic functions <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> as in Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Unique reconstruction from finite samples). ‣ 2 Identifying Analytic Neural Networks from Probe evaluations ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, but we will assume that we are only interested in a compact input domain <math id="S6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> with non-empty interior, and a compact parameter domain <math id="S6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{q}</annotation></semantics></math>. Accordingly, we are interested in the function space
<math id="S6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^{m}):=\left\{f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^{m}):=\left\{f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>
which is a subset of the set of all continuous functions from <math id="S6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, endowed with the infinity norm <math id="S6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|f_{\theta}\|_{\infty}=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\|f(x,\theta)\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|f_{\theta}\|_{\infty}=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\|f(x,\theta)\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. A functional <math id="S6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda:\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^{m})\to\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda:\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^{m})\to\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous, if it is continuous with respect to the distance induced by this norm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our first result uses Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Unique reconstruction from finite samples). ‣ 2 Identifying Analytic Neural Networks from Probe evaluations ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> to show that for general analytic models with <math id="S6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, <math id="S6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2q+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2q+1</annotation></semantics></math> final-layer probes are sufficient for universality:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem6" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 6</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Universality of probe-based learning)<span id="Thmtheorem6.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">With the assumptions listed above, let <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda:\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^{m})\to\mathbb{R}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda:\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}^{m})\to\mathbb{R}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> be a continuous functional. Then there exists <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1},\ldots,p_{2q+1}\in\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1},\ldots,p_{2q+1}\in\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall\,\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">∀</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall\,\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists an MLP <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{\mathrm{MLP}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>MLP</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{\mathrm{MLP}}</annotation></semantics></math> such that
<math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}||\Lambda(f_{\theta})-\phi_{\mathrm{MLP}}\left(f_{\theta}(p_{1}),\ldots,f_{\theta}(p_{2q+1})\right)||&lt;\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>sup</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>MLP</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}||\Lambda(f_{\theta})-\phi_{\mathrm{MLP}}\left(f_{\theta}(p_{1}),\ldots,f_{\theta}(p_{2q+1})\right)||&lt;\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math></span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">When using hidden probes, we can obtain universality using our model <span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> with a significantly smaller number of probes, due to our identifiability results:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem7" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 7</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Universality of <span id="Thmtheorem7.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span>)<span id="Thmtheorem7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmtheorem7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">With our previous notation, assume that</span></p>
<ol id="S6.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S6.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(x;\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x;\theta)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is an MLP architecture with analytic, injective, non-polynomial activation, and maximal width </span><math id="S6.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">max</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{max}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">, and denote </span><math id="S6.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=d_{\text{max}}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">max</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=d_{\text{max}}+1</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">. Or</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(x;\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x;\theta)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is a pure softmax MHA stack with </span><math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> dimensional inputs and at most </span><math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">
heads per layer. Set
</span><math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=d(2H+1)+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=d(2H+1)+1</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="Thmtheorem7.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem7.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Then, if <math id="Thmtheorem7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\subseteq\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>⊆</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\subseteq\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> is a compact subspace of the parameters that does not intersect an appropriate Lebesgue-null set <math id="Thmtheorem7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>, there exist <math id="Thmtheorem7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> probes, and a hidden probe model <math id="Thmtheorem7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}_{\textsc{HiddenProbe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}_{\textsc{HiddenProbe}}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that
<math id="Thmtheorem7.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sup_{\theta\in K}\left\|\Lambda(f_{\theta})-\mathcal{\mathcal{}}H_{\textsc{HiddenProbe}}(\theta)\right\|_{2}&lt;\epsilon." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>sup</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo lspace="0em">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sup_{\theta\in K}\left\|\Lambda(f_{\theta})-\mathcal{\mathcal{}}H_{\textsc{HiddenProbe}}(\theta)\right\|_{2}&lt;\epsilon.</annotation></semantics></math></span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We restate formal versions of the above theorems and prove them in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Learning Functionals and Operators from Probes ‣ Appendix B Proof of Technical results ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>, together with guarantees on operator learning from probes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> for weight space lerning tasks and compare with other prominent baselines. To understand the influence of multi-layer probes, we put a special emphasis on comparison with ProbeGen, which is a successful method relying only on final layer probes. We will show that <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> typically outperforms ProbeGen and other weight space and probe-based models on weight space learning baselines.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">INR classification</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this setting, each input network is an MLP trained as an implicit neural representation (INR) of a single image, and the goal is to predict the class of the represented image directly from the network. We evaluate on the MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 (singke and augmented views). The INR networks across datasets contain two hidden layers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In Table <a href="#S7.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ INR classification ‣ 7 Experiments ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we compare <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> against the baselines: ScaleGMN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalogeropoulos et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, NG-T and Neural Graphs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, NFT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>, MAGEP-NFN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and ProbeGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. A complete comparison with all available methods is provided in Table <a href="#A4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ D.2 Full INR Classification Comparison ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T1" class="ltx_table">
<div id="S7.T1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:397.5pt;height:85.8pt;vertical-align:-40.7pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-26.3pt,5.7pt) scale(0.883109667902984,0.883109667902984) ;">
<table id="S7.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S7.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As observed, <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> achieves the best performance on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, and the second-best performance on augmented CIFAR-10. <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> It outperforms ProbeGen everywhere, highlighting the importance of having hidden layer information. <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3)</span> Probegen comes second in <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3/4</annotation></semantics></math> datasets, proving the efficacy of probe-based learning in general</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Test accuracy prediction</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next evaluate <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> on the model accuracy prediction task. In this setting, the input is a CNN trained for image classification, and the goal is to predict its test accuracy directly from the network. We evaluate on the MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10-GS, and CIFAR-10-WP benchmarks, using Kendall’s correltion(<math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>) as the evaluation metric. In Table <a href="#S7.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Test accuracy prediction ‣ 7 Experiments ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we compare against a representative set of strong baselines: NFN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>, ScaleGMN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalogeropoulos et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, NG-T and Neural Graphs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kofinas et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, DNG-Encoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and ProbeGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahana et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. A complete comparison with all available methods is provided in Table <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ D.3 Full Test-Accuracy Prediction Comparison ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The networks in the MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10-GS benchmarks contain three hidden layers, whereas CIFAR-10-WP contains heterogeneous architectures with up to four hidden layers. <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> achieves the best performance on all five benchmarks and outperforms ProbeGen in every case.</p>
</div>

<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As observed: <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> is the best across all datasets, and probegen comes second in <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4/5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4/5</annotation></semantics></math> datasets. <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> In Cifar-WP where the model architecture varies, probe-based models significantly outperform weight space models since they are more robust to architectural changes.</p>

<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> on test-accuracy prediction for Transformers trained on MNIST and AGNews. Performance for the fuill dataset is shown in Table <a href="#S7.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Transformer Accuracy Prediction. ‣ 7 Experiments ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.Following the evaluation protocol of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al. (2026)</a></cite>, we additionally report results across different accuracy thresholds in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 Transformer Accuracy Prediction Across Thresholds ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a> in tables <a href="#A4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ D.4 Transformer Accuracy Prediction Across Thresholds ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>,<a href="#A4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ D.4 Transformer Accuracy Prediction Across Thresholds ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>

<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Varying performance with the number of probes</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the first part of the experiments, we showed that using the intermediate layers adds significant empirical improvement. Now we want to see how the performance of the probe-based models, namely ProbeGen and <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span>, changes as we vary the number of probes. We compare <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> with ProbeGen using <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\in\{16,32,64,128,256\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\in\{16,32,64,128,256\}</annotation></semantics></math> probes. We take seed 0 results for all plots. Results are in <a href="#S7.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Varying performance with the number of probes ‣ 7 Experiments ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.33901v2/combined.svg" id="S7.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/175;" width="548" height="175"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Performance of HiddenProbe and ProbeGen as the number of probes <math id="S7.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> varies. FMNIST INR classification is evaluated by test accuracy, while regression tasks are evaluated by test Kendall’s <math id="S7.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. Higher is better in all panels.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We make the following observations: <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> generally improves as the probe count increases. Such a trend is also observed for ProbeGen but to a weaker extent <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> is comparable to, or better than, ProbeGen at a smaller ( <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="0.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> or less) probe count. This supports the efficiency of including hidden layer information in probe-based learning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Additional Information</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In all our experiments, <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> uses the same number of parameters as ProbeGen (see <a href="#A4.SS5" title="D.5 Number of parameters comparison ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.5</span></a> for a complete parameter count comparison). A runtime comparison of <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span>, ProbeGen, and other DWS models is provided in Section <a href="#A4.SS6" title="D.6 Time measurement ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.6</span></a>. Synthetic experiments evaluating model reconstruction from finite probes are presented in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Function-level reconstruction on synthetic neural networks ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Finite Probes Suffice: Identifiability and Universality for Weight-Space Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we have done a rigorous theoretical analysis of function-level identification of neural networks from probes. We have shown that one can use probe-based methods to identify a neural network from its outputs and also design universal approximators to learn properties of the neural net from probes. Across architectures like MLPs and Multi head attention blocks, we have shown that this identification can be done with much less number of probes if hidden layer information is incorporated, and we have accordingly proposed <span id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span>, which learns properties of neural nets from full hidden traces. Our experiments demonstrate consistent improvements of <span id="S8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HiddenProbe</span> over ProbeGen and strong weight-space baselines across diverse tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance in several. We also demonstrated that incorporating hidden-layer information enables our models to match or surpass ProbeGen using substantially fewer probes, often requiring only half as many. Together, these results establish hidden-layer probing as an effective approach to learning neural functionals across different architectures and tasks. An interesting direction of future work could be designing such methods for larger architectures like language models or diffusion kernels.</p>
</div>
</section>
